content: Witch-hazel, scientifically known as Hamamelis, is a genus that includes four species of flowering plants within the family Hamamelidaceae. Two of these species, Hamamelis virginiana and Hamamelis vernalis, are native to North America, while Hamamelis japonica is found in Japan, and Hamamelis mollis is native to China. These plants are typically deciduous shrubs, though they can occasionally grow into small trees, reaching heights of 3 to 8 meters, and in rare cases, up to 12 meters. The leaves of witch-hazel are alternately arranged, oval in shape, and measure between 4 to 16 cm in length and 3 to 11 cm in width. The edges of the leaves may be smooth or slightly wavy. The genus name, Hamamelis, translates to together with fruit, which refers to the unique characteristic of the plant where its fruit, flowers, and the buds for the following year’s leaves all appear on the branches simultaneously—a rare trait among trees. The flowers of witch-hazel bloom on leafless stems during the winter, which is why the plant is sometimes referred to as Winterbloom. Each flower consists of four slender, strap-like petals that are 1 to 2 cm long and can range in color from pale to dark yellow, orange, or red. The fruit is a two-part capsule, approximately 1 cm in length, containing a single glossy black seed, about 5 mm in size, in each part. When the fruit matures in the autumn, about eight months after flowering, the capsule splits open explosively, ejecting the seeds with enough force to travel distances of up to 10 meters. This characteristic has earned the plant another nickname, Snapping Hazel. Witch-hazel species serve as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, such as the Feathered Thorn moth. The name witch originates from the Middle English word wiche, derived from the Old English wice, meaning pliant or bendable. The term hazel is associated with the historical use of the plant’s twigs as divining rods, similar to the use of hazel twigs in England. A closely related tree, the Persian ironwood, was previously classified as Hamamelis persica but is now placed in its own genus as Parrotia persica due to its flowers lacking petals. Other related genera include Parrotiopsis, Fothergilla, and Sycopsis, all of which belong to the Hamamelidaceae family. Despite its name, witch-hazel is not closely related to true hazels. Cultivation and Uses Witch-hazel is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant, valued for its clusters of vibrant yellow to orange-red flowers that begin to bloom in the autumn, often coinciding with or slightly preceding the shedding of its leaves, and continue flowering throughout the winter. Numerous cultivars have been developed for use as garden shrubs, many of which are hybrids derived from Hamamelis japonica and Hamamelis mollis, collectively known as Hamamelis × intermedia. The bark and leaves of witch-hazel possess astringent properties, and their extracts, commonly referred to as witch-hazel, are used in various medicinal applications. These extracts are frequently included in aftershave lotions and topical treatments for bruises and insect bites. Witch-hazel is also a key active ingredient in many medications designed to treat hemorrhoids. Additionally, the seeds of the plant contain a significant amount of oil and are edible.
